evidence.label: The abelianity conjecture for special compact Kähler manifolds
Two-step monodromy of special quasi-projective varieties
A conditional abelianity theorem for special fourfold pairs with a half-weight divisor

headline: Special compact Kähler manifolds claim virtually abelian fundamental groups in every dimension, as Campana predicted.
scope: Special compact Kähler manifolds of any dimension; linear images for special quasi-projective varieties; one class of fourfold root orbifolds.
plain: The fundamental group of a space records its loops. Campana predicted that special compact Kähler manifolds have fundamental groups that are abelian after a finite cover. The first paper claims to prove this in every dimension. A second paper claims that, for open special varieties, matrix images are nilpotent of class at most two. A third paper uses the first to treat certain four-dimensional orbifolds.
doesNot: This does not bound the index of the abelian subgroup or cover orbifolds beyond the one-divisor fourfold case.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: F. Campana, who introduced special varieties and their framework
scorecard.significanceWhy: If correct, it settles a central prediction of Campana’s classification program in every dimension.

explanation:
Take a closed curve of genus g, with B points removed. Count 2g − 2 + B. For a smooth curve, specialness means this count is at most zero[13]. A doughnut-shaped elliptic curve has g = 1 and B = 0, so the count is 0. It is special. The sphere with two points removed gives −2 + 2 = 0, also special. The sphere with three points removed gives −2 + 3 = 1. It is not special[13].

Now look at loops. The fundamental group of a space records the loops in it, up to deformation, with joining loops as the operation. For the doughnut it is pairs of whole numbers, and the order of joining does not matter. Such a group is abelian. For a curve with two or more holes, the group is far from abelian. So, among closed curves, special shapes have abelian loop groups.

Campana’s abelianity conjecture predicts this pattern in every dimension. A special compact Kähler manifold should have a fundamental group that becomes abelian after passing to a finite unramified cover[1]. Such a group is called virtually abelian. Here special means, roughly, that no holomorphic forms detect a map onto a base of general type[2]. A compact Kähler manifold is a compact complex space with a compatible way to measure lengths.

The first paper claims to prove the conjecture in every dimension[3]. The claim covers the whole fundamental group. It needs no assumption of linearity, residual finiteness, projectivity or a particular Kodaira dimension[4]. The finite index may depend on the manifold[4]. One consequence covers Kodaira dimension zero, a standard class that includes Calabi–Yau manifolds. Campana had shown such manifolds are special. So their fundamental groups are virtually abelian[5].

What was known before? Campana and Claudon proved the conjecture for compact Kähler threefolds[6]. For manifolds with zero first Chern class, Beauville’s decomposition already gave the answer[7]. Results on linear quotients were also known. But an infinite group need not have an infinite linear image[8]. A linear image means a copy of the group acting by matrices. Controlling those leftover quotients is the key obstacle for a claim about the whole group[8]. The paper’s new step gets enough positivity from holomorphic tensors with values in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces[9].

The second paper moves to open, non-compact varieties. There, nonabelian groups of a mild kind can appear. Take the Heisenberg group of 3 × 3 upper-triangular whole-number matrices with ones on the diagonal. Let a have a 1 in the top middle, and b a 1 at the right of the middle row. Their commutator, a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹, has a single 1 in the top-right corner. That commutator commutes with both a and b. A group where every commutator commutes with everything has nilpotency class at most two[10].

The second paper claims an independent proof about such groups. Take a smooth special quasi-projective variety. Every complex matrix image of its fundamental group is virtually of class at most two[11]. Cao, Deng, Hacon and Păun announced this conclusion first, and the paper gives them priority[12]. The bound is optimal. An earlier example has a Heisenberg-type group that is not virtually abelian[14].

The third paper treats a root orbifold. This is a fourfold X with one smooth divisor D counted with weight one half. The paper claims virtual abelianity of the full orbifold fundamental group when this orbifold is special[15]. It is conditional: it assumes the first paper’s theorem[16]. It builds a special eightfold whose fundamental group maps onto the needed group[17].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for these papers in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked them. The third paper depends on the first. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proof holds. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. The orbifold result is conditional on the first paper, and the linear-image result was announced earlier by other authors.

glossary.meaning: The group of loops in a space, up to deformation, with joining loops as the operation.
A group in which the order of combining two elements never matters.
Having an abelian subgroup of finite index, or abelian after a finite cover.
Having no holomorphic forms that detect a map onto a base of general type.
A compact complex manifold with a compatible way to measure lengths and areas.
A group property: every commutator commutes with every element.
A space in which a chosen divisor is counted with a fractional weight, here one half.
